title: Load Balancing
oneLiner: How a load balancer spreads requests across servers, and what goes wrong when requests differ in cost or a server dies.
keyTakeaway: A load balancer lets you add servers to handle more traffic and survive losing one, but only if the servers are stateless (they keep no per-user data in their own memory between requests) and the balancer runs health checks. Round robin is fine for uniform requests; least connections or power of two choices copes much better when some requests are expensive.
explanation:
A load balancer sits in front of a group of identical servers and gives clients one address. Each incoming request goes to one of the servers, so you can handle more traffic by adding servers (horizontal scaling) and keep serving when one of them fails. Almost every design in an interview has one in front of the application tier.

The choice of server is the algorithm. Round robin takes turns; random picks any server. Both spread requests evenly by count, which is fine when every request costs about the same. When some requests are expensive, a server that picked up a few slow ones keeps getting its turn and short requests wait behind them. Least connections sends each request to the server with the fewest requests in flight, which steers around busy servers. Power of two choices picks two servers at random and takes the less busy one; it gets most of the benefit without checking every server, which matters when there are many load balancer instances that can't share exact counts. Weighted variants give bigger servers a larger share. Turn on heavy requests in the demo and compare the p95 latency (the time 95% of requests finish within) of short requests across algorithms.

Health checks are how the balancer learns that a server is gone: it requests something like /health every few seconds and removes servers that fail. Kill a server with health checks off and every request sent to it fails. With least connections it's worse, because a dead server that refuses connections instantly always looks the least busy, so it attracts nearly all the traffic. With health checks on, you still lose the requests sent in the gap before the next check.

Layer 4 load balancers route TCP connections by IP address and port, without looking inside; they're fast and simple. Layer 7 load balancers understand HTTP, so they can route by path or header (send /api to one pool and /images to another), terminate TLS, and retry failed requests, at some extra cost per request.

Sticky sessions send the same user to the same server every time, usually by a cookie. They're a workaround for servers that keep session state in memory, and they undermine the whole point: that server's users lose their sessions when it dies, and load can't be rebalanced. The better answer is stateless application servers that keep sessions in a shared store such as Redis or in a signed token, so any server can handle any request.

The load balancer itself must not become a single point of failure. The usual setup is an active-passive pair sharing a floating IP address: if the active one stops sending heartbeats, the passive one takes over the address. Cloud load balancers do this for you. Across regions, DNS-based global load balancing returns the address of the nearest healthy region, and each region then has its own load balancers.
